where: Section 3, table row 'Half-wave | R, or discontinuous RL'
problem: The table gives the pure-resistance value (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α) for a half-wave circuit with a discontinuous RL load. With any inductance the current does not stop at π; it reaches zero at an extinction angle β > π, and Vdc = (Vm/2π)(cos α − cos β), which is smaller than (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α). Section 1 of the same chapter says exactly this ('the output has a negative part and Vdc falls'), so the table contradicts the text.
fix: Split the row. Half-wave, R load: Vdc = (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α). Half-wave, discontinuous RL: Vdc = (Vm/2π)(cos α − cos β) with β the extinction angle, a value between (Vm/π)cos α and (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α).

where: Section 2, last sentence of the R-load paragraph
problem: 'otherwise it is discontinuous and the cosine formula over-predicts the output' has the sign of the error reversed. When the current is discontinuous, the actual average is higher than (2Vm/π)cos α, not lower; the chapter's own numbers show it (at α = 60°, R load gives 0.477 Vm against 0.318 Vm from the cosine formula), and the general rule for a phase-controlled converter is that discontinuous conduction raises Vdc above the continuous-conduction value.
fix: Write: 'otherwise it is discontinuous, conduction ends at an extinction angle before the next firing instant, and the actual Vdc is higher than the continuous-current formula predicts (for example (Vm/π)(1 + cos α) for a pure resistance, against (2Vm/π)cos α).'

problem: 'Below the boundary the continuous-current formula over-predicts Vdc' repeats the reversed claim. Discontinuous operation gives a higher average output, so the continuous-current formula under-predicts Vdc for α < 90° and gives too large a negative value for α > 90°.
fix: Say that below the boundary the continuous-current formula under-predicts Vdc (the discontinuous output is higher, i.e. less negative in inverter mode), and the actual value must be found from the extinction angle.

problem: 'an RLE load whose back EMF is smaller than the negative output' reads as a magnitude comparison. The condition is a numerical one: E must satisfy E = Vdc − IdcR, so the back EMF must be more negative than the converter output, that is of larger magnitude. As written, most students will take the opposite condition.
fix: Write: 'an RLE load whose back EMF is more negative than the average output (its magnitude is larger), so the load itself drives the current round in the same direction.'

where: Section 1 and Quiz Q1, definition of natural commutation point
problem: The term is defined here as the instant the device would start conducting if it were a diode. Many textbooks reserve 'natural commutation' for the instant a conducting device turns off at current zero (for a half-wave RL circuit that is β, not the start of conduction), so a student may be marked down for this wording.
fix: Call the reference the natural firing point (the instant the device would start conducting if it were a diode), and add one line: natural commutation is the later instant when the device current falls to zero and it turns off; in the bridge circuits here the two instants coincide.

problem: The lead says the chapter covers R, RL and RLE loads, but RLE appears only in one clause and one exam trap: no formula, no example and no table row for a back EMF.
fix: Either drop RLE from the lead, or add one short block giving the RLE conduction condition (conduction starts when vs exceeds E, i.e. α measured from sin⁻¹(E/Vm)) and a table row showing that in discontinuous mode the load terminal voltage equals E while the current is zero.
